## Boise State: HR Now Reports to the President {.section-slide data-background-color="#102a43"}

## On the Horizon with President Hahn

## Compensation Strategies

::::::::: {.system-grid .roomy-grid .cb-strats}
::: system-item
[Single rate]{.card-heading}

<p>Everyone in the job is paid the same; across-the-board cost-of-living raises tied to the Consumer Price Index</p>
:::

::: system-item
[Time based]{.card-heading}

<p>Steps based on longevity; "make no distinction between high performers and low performers"</p>
:::

::: system-item
[Productivity based]{.card-heading}

<p>Pay tied to a preset output goal; works only when outputs are "unambiguous and easily measured"</p>
:::

::: system-item
[Person based]{.card-heading}

<p>Pay follows the person's competencies, experience, education, and seniority, not the position</p>
:::

::: system-item
[Pay-for-performance]{.card-heading}

<p>Increases "dependent on performance appraisal ratings, rather than on years of experience"</p>
:::

::: system-item
[Equity adjustments]{.card-heading}

<p>When an audit shows a job is paid below market, or similar jobs are paid very differently</p>
:::
:::::::::

::: {.question-bar .fragment}
Which of these have you been paid under?
:::

## Activity: Employee or Manager? {.activity-slide data-background-color="#176b87"}

::: activity-prompt
Single rate, time based, productivity based, person based, pay-for-performance.
:::

1.  As an employee, which do you prefer and why?
2.  As a manager, which do you prefer and why?
3.  Does your answer change when you switch roles? Why?

::: activity-close
10 minutes in groups
:::

## Step Pay and Pay-for-Performance

::::: {.compare .jd .roomy .rs-quote}
::: compare-side
[Step-based pay]{.card-heading}

Easy to operationalize, "increments are predictable and transparent, and they do not encourage competition among coworkers."

But "for those whose performance is motivated by raises, the reliability of increments removes the incentive to perform at a higher-than-average level."
:::

::: {.compare-side .accent .fragment}
[Pay-for-performance]{.card-heading}

"While the theory is that pay-for-performance places the decision of how hard to work on the employee, in fact, in most jobs it hands more discretion to the supervisor, who has leverage over the employee."
:::
:::::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
Effective pay-for-performance depends on fair and effective performance appraisals. (Week 9)
:::

::: source-line
Guy & Sowa instructor manual, Ch. 7 key words.
:::

## Taylor and Scientific Management (1911)

```{=html}
<div class="cb-taylor">
<div class="cb-taylor-quote"><p>“One of the very first requirements for a man who is fit to handle pig iron as a regular occupation is that he shall be so stupid and so phlegmatic that he more nearly resembles in his mental make-up the ox than any other type.”</p></div>
<div class="cb-taylor-stats">
<div class="stat fragment"><span class="stat-number">12½ → 47½</span><p>Tons of pig iron loaded per man per day, Bethlehem Steel</p></div>
<div class="stat fragment"><span class="stat-number">$1.15 → $1.85</span><p>“Schmidt’s” daily wage for doing it Taylor’s way</p></div>
</div>
</div>
```

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
Taylor believed workers were motivated primarily by pay: pay them according to productivity.
:::

::: source-line
Frederick W. Taylor, *The Principles of Scientific Management* (1911). The pursuit of "the one best way"; efficiency and economy.
:::

## The Human Relations Movement

::: {.timeline .cb-hr}
<div class="tl-step cb-hr-taylor"><span class="tl-year">1911</span><span class="card-heading">Taylor</span><p>Scientific management: the one best way; pay for output</p></div>
<div class="tl-step"><span class="tl-year">1918</span><span class="card-heading">Mary Parker Follett</span><p>The “law of the situation”; authority as power with, not over</p></div>
<div class="tl-step accent-step"><span class="tl-year">1924–32</span><span class="card-heading">Mayo: Hawthorne studies</span><p>Attention and informal groups raise productivity: money is not everything</p></div>
<div class="tl-step"><span class="tl-year">1938</span><span class="card-heading">Chester Barnard</span><p>The organization as a cooperative system; the “zone of indifference”</p></div>
<div class="tl-step"><span class="tl-year">1943</span><span class="card-heading">Abraham Maslow</span><p>A hierarchy of needs explains why people respond to different incentives</p></div>
<div class="tl-step"><span class="tl-year">1960</span><span class="card-heading">Douglas McGregor</span><p>Theory X and Theory Y: what managers assume about workers</p></div>
:::

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
The Hawthorne studies were the first empirical challenge to Taylor's scientific management.
:::

## McGregor: Theory X and Theory Y (1960)

::::: {.compare .jd .roomy .jd-cols}
::: compare-side
[Theory X]{.card-heading}

- The average person dislikes work and will avoid it if they can
- Most people must be coerced, controlled, directed, or threatened with punishment
- The average person prefers to be directed and wants security above all
:::

::: {.compare-side .accent .fragment}
[Theory Y]{.card-heading}

- Effort at work is as natural as play or rest
- Control and threats are not the only ways to bring about effort
- Commitment to objectives is a function of the rewards for achieving them
- Under the right conditions, people seek responsibility
:::
:::::

::: {.question-bar .fragment}
Which theory does step pay assume? Which does pay-for-performance assume?
:::

## Public Service Motivation

::: cb-email
"An individual's predisposition to respond to motives grounded primarily or uniquely in public institutions and organizations."
:::

::: {.system-grid .roomy-grid .cb-psm}
<div class="system-item"><span class="card-heading">Rational</span><p>Participating in policymaking; a need for power and recognition</p></div>
<div class="system-item"><span class="card-heading">Norm-based</span><p>A sense of duty: public service is the right thing to do</p></div>
<div class="system-item"><span class="card-heading">Affective</span><p>Public service feels good: satisfaction from helping the community</p></div>
:::

::: {.jd-note .fragment}
Week 7 callback: in Chattanooga, the "ready to serve?" postcard brought in no more applicants than no postcard at all.
:::

::: source-line
Perry, J. L., & Wise, L. R. (1990). The motivational bases of public service. *Public Administration Review*, 50(3), 367–373 (definition, p. 368).
:::

## Pay-for-Performance and Intrinsic Motivation

::::: {.compare .jd .roomy .rs-quote}
::: compare-side
[Weibel, Rost, and Osterloh (2010)]{.card-heading}

A meta-analysis of experiments plus a vignette study: pay for performance raises effort through extrinsic motivation, but it can crowd out intrinsic motivation. It "is generally more costly as it appears because it almost always produces hidden costs of rewards."
:::

::: {.compare-side .accent .fragment}
[For public managers]{.card-heading}

- Structure work and incentives to account for public service motivation
- Be careful applying private sector pay practices to the public sector
:::
:::::

::: {.question-bar .fragment}
If public employees are motivated by service, what should government pay for?
:::

::: source-line
Weibel, A., Rost, K., & Osterloh, M. (2010). Pay for performance in the public sector—Benefits and (hidden) costs. *JPART*, 20(2), 387–412.
:::

## Classification Systems

::::: {.compare .jd .roomy .jd-cols}
::: compare-side
[Rank-in-position]{.card-heading}

- Salary, benefits, and rank are tied to the position
- Move jobs, and you must qualify for the new grade
- Example: the General Schedule
:::

::: {.compare-side .accent}
[Rank-in-person]{.card-heading}

- Salary, benefits, and rank travel with the person
- Pay reflects competencies, experience, education, performance, seniority
- Examples: the U.S. military, the Foreign Service
:::
:::::

::: jd-note
Alternatives within classification: paybanding and broadbanding, which give managers discretion over pay within a wide band (China Lake, Week 6).
:::

::: {.question-bar .fragment}
Your experiences? Which system are you in now?
:::

## Defined Benefit vs. Defined Contribution

::::: {.compare .jd .roomy .rs-quote}
::: compare-side
[Defined benefit]{.card-heading}

The benefit is "based on a predetermined formula and the employer's fund is responsible for providing the benefit for the lifetime of the retired employee."

**The employer bears the risk.**
:::

::: {.compare-side .accent}
[Defined contribution]{.card-heading}

The benefit "depends on how much they contribute to the plan over time and how financial markets perform."

**The employee bears the risk.**
:::
:::::

::: jd-note
Idaho's PERSI base plan is a defined benefit plan; many Boise State faculty and professional staff are instead in the Optional Retirement Plan (defined contribution). Federal FERS combines a basic annuity (defined benefit), the Thrift Savings Plan (defined contribution), and Social Security.
:::

::: source-line
Guy & Sowa instructor manual, Ch. 7 key words.
:::

## Pay Law and Pay Now {.section-slide data-background-color="#102a43"}

## Major Laws Governing Compensation

:::::::::: {.timeline .cb-laws}
::: tl-step
[1938]{.tl-year}[Fair Labor Standards Act]{.card-heading}

<p>Minimum wage and overtime; exempt vs. nonexempt</p>
:::

::: tl-step
[1949]{.tl-year}[Classification Act]{.card-heading}

<p>Creates the General Schedule; equal pay for substantially equal work</p>
:::

::: tl-step
[1963]{.tl-year}[Equal Pay Act]{.card-heading}

<p>No sex-based wage differences for substantially equal work</p>
:::

::: tl-step
[1964]{.tl-year}[Title VII, Civil Rights Act]{.card-heading}

<p>No pay discrimination by race, color, religion, sex, or national origin</p>
:::

::: tl-step
[1993]{.tl-year}[Family and Medical Leave Act]{.card-heading}

<p>Unpaid, job-protected leave for family and medical reasons</p>
:::

::: {.tl-step .accent-step}
[2009]{.tl-year}[Lilly Ledbetter Fair Pay Act]{.card-heading}

<p>Each discriminatory paycheck is a separate violation</p>
:::

::: tl-step
[2010]{.tl-year}[Affordable Care Act]{.card-heading}

<p>Employer health coverage requirements</p>
:::
::::::::::

::: source-line
Guy & Sowa instructor manual, Ch. 7 key dates.
:::

## Exempt vs. Non-exempt

::::: {.compare .jd .roomy .jd-cols}
::: compare-side
[Exempt]{.card-heading}

- Not covered by the FLSA's overtime provisions
- Executive, professional, or administrative, and meets the criteria
- Generally paid a salary
:::

::: {.compare-side .accent}
[Non-exempt]{.card-heading}

- Overtime for all hours beyond 40 in the work week
- Applies whether paid hourly or salaried
- Public employers may give comp time (at time and a half) instead of cash
:::
:::::

::: {.rs-status .fragment}
**Where it stands in 2026.** Exempt status requires at least \$684 a week (\$35,568 a year). A court vacated the 2024 increase in November 2024; DOL restored the 2019 level May 15, 2026.
:::

::: source-line
29 CFR 541.600 · 29 U.S.C. § 207(o) · *Texas v. U.S. Department of Labor* (E.D. Tex., Nov. 15, 2024) · DOL technical amendment, effective May 15, 2026
:::

## Bringing It Together

::: jd-lead
- Compensation and benefits are essential considerations for all organizations
- Compensation has tangible and intangible effects for people
- There is not one perfect compensation plan. Employers need to consider:
:::

```{=html}
<div class="el-chips cb-chips cb-consider">
<span class="el-chip">Equity</span><span class="el-chip">Fairness</span><span class="el-chip">Ease of administration</span><span class="el-chip">Alignment with the market</span><span class="el-chip">Sustainability</span>
</div>
```

::: {.takeaway .fragment}
The purpose of organizations is to achieve a mission. Compensating people for contributing to this mission is an essential component of achieving high performance.
:::
